pedagogy.summary: Composing 3-D shapes — stacking and combining solids to build new structures and composite shapes — develops through a well-charted progression from unsystematic stacking, through trial-and-error assembly, to composing WITH ANTICIPATION ('I know the cone goes on top'). It is best taught with plentiful block-building using real solids, where the teacher notices and gently nudges children toward the next level — asking them to predict which shape will fit before placing it and to describe their creation by its component solids. Matched building challenges pitched one level ahead move children forward more effectively than jumping straight to the target.
bestPractices: Give rich, open block-building with a range of solids (cubes, prisms, cylinders, cones) and let children build and knock down freely at first.
Nudge toward anticipation: 'Can you see which shape will fit on top before you place it?' — shifting from trial and error to planning.
Pitch challenges one level beyond the child's current building (e.g. from stacking identical blocks to combining a cone on a cylinder), scaffolding then fading support.
Ask the child to describe the composite by its parts — name each component solid and where it sits.
Attend to which faces sit flat: choosing a flat-faced solid for the base keeps a structure stable.
keyRepresentations: Target-picture cards of composites (cone-on-cylinder rocket, cube tower, house)
The stack ('on') relationship; flat-faced base vs rolling curved base
commonMisconceptions: Adds blocks unsystematically and only recognises what it 'looks like' after building — no advance plan (a normal early trajectory level, not a fault).
Builds a composite but describes it only as one whole ('a rocket') and cannot name the component solids or their positions.
Places solids without regard to which faces are flat, so a cone or sphere used as a base makes the structure topple.

learn.summary: Children aged 6–7 learn to compose 3-D shapes by stacking and combining real solids (cubes, prisms, cylinders, cones, spheres) into composite structures. The target skill is a progression: from unsystematic stacking, through trial-and-error assembly, to composing WITH ANTICIPATION — knowing in advance which shape will fit ('the cone goes on top') and naming a build by its component solids and their positions. Hands-on block-building with challenges pitched one level ahead, plus prompts to predict and describe, carries children forward; because this is a procedural, construction-based goal, physical block-building is the core medium. An on-screen 3-D sandbox is an optional supplementary model that preserves stacking, balance and depth, while flat drag-and-combine and matching tasks are useful scaffolds for naming parts but do not exercise balance or anticipation.

activities.title: Build a rocket with real solids
feedback: If the child places shapes at random and names the result only afterwards, do not mark this wrong — it is an expected early level. Offer a challenge one step ahead and prompt 'can you see which shape will fit before you place it?'
If the child names only the whole ('a rocket') but not the parts, take the composite apart and name each solid together, then rebuild it, naming each shape as it goes on.

If the tower topples, look together at which faces rest on the table or on the shape below: a sphere rolls because it has no flat face, a cone balanced on its point has no flat face down, and a piece placed off-centre can tip over. So choose a flat-faced solid (a cube, prism, or cylinder on a flat face) for the base, keep each piece centred, and don't stack anything on a cone's point, rather than blaming the blocks.
Reinforce correct anticipation: when the child reaches for the cone before placing it, confirm the plan aloud ('yes — the cone fits on top of the cylinder').
activities.rationale: Composing is an action: building, balancing and anticipating are exercised by actual construction with solids, not by recognising a finished picture. The documented trajectory runs from trial-and-error, post-hoc recognition to composing with anticipation and advance planning, and the curriculum asks children to compose and model shapes by building from components.
sourceClaims: Composing 3-D shapes develops through levels — Stacker and Same-Shape Stacker (using the 'on' relationship), Piece Assembler and Picture Maker (building components, arches and enclosures by unsystematic trial and error), then Shape Composer (composing with anticipation, understanding what 3-D shape a combination will produce and building systematically).

Shape composition progresses from trial-and-error, post-hoc recognition (Piece Assembler, Picture Maker) to composing with anticipation and advance planning (Shape Composer); teaching contiguous trajectory levels, scaffolded one level ahead, produced greater learning than jumping to the target level (effect size .55).
Kindergarten geometry asks children to compose simple shapes to form larger shapes and to model shapes by building from components.
learnerActions: Offer a set of real 3-D blocks: cubes, a cylinder, a cone, some prisms, and a sphere.
Ask the child to build a rocket by combining shapes so that it stands up.
Before each placement, prompt: 'Which shape will fit on top before you place it? Where will it go and why does it fit?'
After building, ask the child to point to and name each shape used and say where it sits (e.g. 'a cylinder at the bottom, a cone on top').

Try using the sphere as the base (or balancing the cone on its point) and let the child notice that it rolls or will not support more shapes, then choose a flat-faced solid — a cube, prism, or cylinder resting on a flat face — for the base.
activities.intendedInsight: A composite is made of named component solids combined on purpose; resting flat faces down keeps a structure stable, and you can plan which shape fits before placing it rather than only recognising the result afterwards.

activities.title: Challenges pitched one level ahead
feedback: If the challenge is too hard, step back one level and rebuild success before advancing again.
Praise the planning talk ('I'll put the cone on top next'), not just the finished structure.
activities.rationale: Teaching contiguous trajectory levels, scaffolded one level ahead, produced greater learning than jumping to the target level in the cited study.
sourceClaims: Shape composition progresses from trial-and-error, post-hoc recognition (Piece Assembler, Picture Maker) to composing with anticipation and advance planning (Shape Composer); teaching contiguous trajectory levels, scaffolded one level ahead, produced greater learning than jumping to the target level (effect size .55).
learnerActions: Watch how the child currently builds to judge their level (free stacking, trial-and-error assembly, or anticipating).
Set a building challenge just one step beyond that level — for example, from stacking identical cubes to combining a cone on a cylinder, or from trial-and-error assembly to predicting the next piece.
Scaffold with prompts and modelling, then gradually fade support as the child succeeds.
Repeat the same build and ask the child to say each shape as they add it.
activities.intendedInsight: Children advance most when the next task is just ahead of their current building, with support that fades, rather than jumping straight to the final target.

activities.title: On-screen 3-D building sandbox (optional)
feedback: If a build topples because of a rolling base, let the child retry with a flat-faced base and connect the failure to the face that rolled.
Use the tap-to-name feature to help a child who sees only the whole begin to decompose it into component solids.
activities.rationale: An interactive 3-D build space preserves the stacking, balance and depth that define 3-D composition, which flat 2-D drag-and-combine loses. It is offered as a supplementary medium option alongside physical blocks, not as a replacement for hands-on construction, and the cited sources do not establish that either medium is superior.
learnerActions: Drag 3-D solids into a build space and snap a cone onto a cylinder to make a rocket.
Try placing a sphere as a base; if the sandbox simulates gravity, watch whether it rolls and the tower falls, and talk about which faces must sit flat.
Before placing a piece, respond to the prompt 'which shape will fit on top?'
Tap the finished build to hear its component solids named in order ('cylinder… cone').
activities.intendedInsight: A 3-D model lets a child stack, combine and test balance, plan placements and have parts named — exercising the composing skill, including why a solid with no flat face, such as a sphere, makes a poor base.

activities.title: Match composites to their parts (naming activity)
feedback: If the child names only the whole, point to each region and name the solid, then ask them to repeat which part is the cylinder and which is the cone.
Treat this as a recognition and vocabulary scaffold; follow it with actual building so the child plans and balances, not just recognises.
activities.rationale: Matching and tap-to-name references can build and check part-naming vocabulary, but they support and check recognition rather than the act of composing with anticipation or managing balance; no cited source establishes a matching task as necessary or sufficient for the composing skill.
learnerActions: Show a picture or model of a composite (e.g. a cone-on-cylinder rocket, a cube tower, a house).
Ask the child to choose which component solids make it up and where each one sits.
Optionally use a reference image where tapping a part names it (rocket = cone + cylinder).
activities.intendedInsight: A composite can be decomposed into named component solids, each in a particular position — reinforcing part-naming vocabulary.

constraints: The core objective is composing with anticipation and describing a build by its component solids and their positions — this is a procedural curriculum goal that requires actual construction, with physical block-building as the core medium, not only recognising a finished shape.
Treat unsystematic stacking and post-hoc recognition as an expected early developmental level, not an error to drill or mark wrong; advance with one-step-ahead challenges.
Matching tasks and tap-to-name reference images support/check part-naming vocabulary (recognition) but do not themselves elicit independent construction, balancing, or advance planning.
Flat 2-D drag-and-combine can name parts but cannot convey which faces sit flat or how a tower balances; use it only as a naming scaffold.

Balance depends partly on resting flat faces down: a sphere (no flat face) rolls; a cone stands steadily base-down, but it topples if balanced on its point, rolls if laid on its side, and cannot hold a block on its apex; a cube, prism, or cylinder resting on a flat face is stable on its own, although a tower can still topple if pieces are placed off-centre or it gets too tall and narrow. Use this to explain why a flat-faced base is a good choice, not as a claim about any specific product.
A fixed labelled picture can still teach part-naming as a reference, but cannot be manipulated to practise stacking or anticipation.
reviewNotes: This is an agent semantic rewrite of saved teaching research without fresh source verification; sources were not re-fetched. All activities are research-informed proposals, not validated interventions.
The cited effect size (.55) and the trajectory-level descriptions are copied from the original source claims and were not independently re-verified here.

The original marked an on-screen 3-D sandbox as 'ideal' and dialogue/2-D as poor; these catalog fit rankings have been removed. Comparative-necessity framing ('dialogue cannot substitute', 'a static picture cannot teach') has been softened to scoped affordance/limit statements. The cited sources establish the developmental trajectory and one-level-ahead scaffolding, not the superiority of any particular medium.

Physical blocks and an on-screen model offer different experiences (real tactile balance vs. resettable digital trials); physical construction is the curriculum-required core medium and neither is asserted as universally necessary over the other for every learner.

The original row stated a cone used as a base topples; this was clarified because a cone can sit stably on its flat circular face. The instability is specific to a sphere (no flat face) or a cone balanced on its point / used to support further stacking on its apex.

probeDeeper: Before you place that shape — can you tell me where it will go and why it fits?
Point to each shape you used and name it — which is the cylinder, which is the cone?
Why does the tower fall when the cone is at the bottom? Which shapes make a good base?
Can you build the same rocket again, telling me each shape as you add it?
assess.correctAnswer: Selects and stacks solids with anticipation to make the intended composite (e.g. a cylinder body with a cone on top), keeps it stable by resting flat faces down, and describes the result by naming its component solids and their positions ('a cylinder at the bottom, a cone on top').

errorPatterns.pattern: Adds blocks unsystematically and recognises what the structure 'looks like' only after building — no advance plan for the composite
errorPatterns.nextMove: Do NOT drill or mark this 'wrong' — it is an expected early level; offer building challenges one step ahead and prompt 'can you see which shape will fit before you place it?'
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Places shapes at random and names the result post hoc; cannot say in advance which shape will fit

errorPatterns.pattern: Builds a composite but describes it only as one whole ('a rocket') and cannot name the component solids or their positions
errorPatterns.nextMove: Take the composite apart and name each solid, then rebuild it naming each shape as it goes on
errorPatterns.revealedBy: Names the whole structure but not the cylinder/cone parts

errorPatterns.pattern: Places solids without regard to which faces are flat, so the structure will not balance — a cone or sphere used as a base makes it topple
errorPatterns.nextMove: Notice together which faces are flat and rest on the table, and choose a flat-faced solid for the base
errorPatterns.revealedBy: The tower falls; the child blames the blocks rather than the choice of base

responseLevels.gap: Stacks blocks unsystematically and names only the whole ('a tower'); cannot say which solids make it up.
responseLevels.full: Selects and combines solids with anticipation to make a planned composite, keeps it stable by resting flat faces down, and describes the result by its component solids and their positions.
responseLevels.partial: Builds the intended composite, often by trial and error, and names some parts, but does not choose shapes with anticipation or explain why a shape fits or balances.

assess.diagnosticPrompt: Here are some 3-D blocks — cubes, a cylinder, a cone, some prisms. Build me a rocket by putting shapes together so it stands up. As you build, and when you finish, tell me which shapes you used and where each one is.
assess.whatMakesItDiscriminate: Watching the build separates the child who composes with anticipation ('I know the cone goes on top', reaching for it before placing) from the trial-and-error assembler who stacks unsystematically and recognises the result only afterwards. Asking the child to name the parts exposes whether they can decompose the composite into its component solids rather than seeing it as one undifferentiated 'rocket'.
